item.title: The Things Nobody Tells You About Training for Your First Marathon
item.dc:creator: Margaret Cole
item.description: Five things I wish I’d known before my first marathon.
item.content:encoded:
I ran a marathon almost a month ago. If you know me personally, this is 100% old news because obviously training became my entire personality. If you’re not a runner, you probably have some vague idea of what this training may have looked like—perhaps you simply pictured me waking up at the crack of dawn and by some unknown supernatural force, enduring the pain of putting one foot in front of the other for hours on end before going about my normal day. And to an extent, this is somewhat accurate. But underneath the surface, there is so much more that goes into training for and successfully running your first marathon. If I were to do it all over again, these are the things I wish I would’ve known from the beginning:

1. Running is actually quite expensive

To many, running is perceived as the cheapest sport you could do. Literally all you need in order to run is a pair of shoes, right?

Wrong.

When you get to the marathon distance, or even the half marathon distance, there are so many additional costs that will creep up on you and before you know it, you’ve spent hundreds before your first race. In addition to a quality pair of shoes (check out this article for my favorite pair), you will also need to sign up for your race. Running has become so popular since COVID-19 that race prices have also shot through the roof. I signed up for the Marine Corps Marathon over six months in advance and it still cost $267! And the longer you wait to sign up, the more expensive it will be.

There is also the cost of traveling to the marathon you decide to sign up for, if there isn’t one nearby that’s available. Thankfully, I did not have to travel to mine, but many people today do, especially if you’re eyeing a World Major (more on that in another article soon). If you have to travel, that means buying plane tickets or paying for gas and potentially having to stay in a hotel as well.

Race logistics aside, there are numerous additional expenses you will have to make throughout the course of your training that you may not have anticipated beforehand. Once you start getting closer to running double-digit mile runs, you’ll want to have some sort of device for carrying water, unless you’re one of the very few who can somehow survive on pure vibes and water fountains. I had to buy multiple different water carriers before I found the one that worked best for me. I started with a running vest before switching to a handheld water bottle, and so I probably spent close to $100 on just figuring out how to carry water while running.

When you begin running these longer distances, you will also need to start buying proper fuel to bring with you. There have been numerous studies on the impacts of gels on running performance, but putting it simply, on your longer runs, you need to fuel mid-run in order to properly perform and recover well, because running on empty makes both the run and the days after it harder.

When I started training for longer-distance running, I went as long as possible without buying gels but eventually, it got to a point where, as a result of just fueling on water, my vision would begin to go blurry and I could feel my energy drop massively towards the end of my runs. I would recommend buying a pack of energy gels before you run your first 9+ mile run. Once your long runs start to enter the 14+ mile range, you will likely feel the effects of having to buy gels so frequently since you’ll likely be consuming 3+ on each long run, but they are necessary, unless you find a healthy alternative.

The last expense you might not have anticipated when it comes to training for your first marathon is the cost of electrolytes. Electrolytes, similar to gels, are a highly necessary source of fuel while on long runs (and after long runs). Electrolytes come in many forms and some gels even have electrolytes in them, but electrolyte tablets, packets, or powder is something you will likely need to buy sooner or later during your marathon journey. At one point in the middle of my training, I ran out of electrolyte powder and I actually started making my own electrolyte mix to put in my water, since electrolyte powder is primarily just salt and sugar, and this worked for several of my long runs, before I decided to go back to buying electrolyte powder.

Many of these expenses are fairly cheap, however, they do add up over time, and so it is worth considering before you sign up for a marathon if you have the budget to sustain months of training.

2. The season that your marathon takes place in will impact your entire training plan

When I signed up for the Marine Corps Marathon, which occurred the last weekend of October, I completely overlooked the fact that the majority of my training would take place during the summer. Depending on where you live, this could make for an absolutely brutal 3-6 months, depending on how long you decide to train for. My training block was 26 weeks (6 months) starting in late April and so I literally only experienced roughly 3-4 weeks total of tolerable weather. The other 22 weeks were frankly the hardest physical challenge of my life, aside from the marathon itself. Despite running in the dark before the sun rose many mornings, the low temperature was often in the low 70s with 90+ percent humidity. This meant that on runs that lasted several hours, it was not uncommon for my run to end having hit close to 80 degrees.

Do not underestimate the impact of the heat and humidity on your training. Even as someone who has been running for the majority of her life, my performance was still massively affected by the weather in ways I couldn’t imagine beforehand. There were many days when I cut my runs short from near heat exhaustion and I could probably count the number of times on one hand that I didn’t come home completely dripping sweat even from a 3-mile run.

Now one important note to make here is that my brutal summer training absolutely paid off on race day when I ran a time faster than I could have ever anticipated; however, it is seriously worth evaluating if the payoff is worth it.

This is my perspective on training for a fall marathon, but you can come back in six months to hear my review of training for a spring marathon instead since I’m quickly approaching the start of my London Marathon training block.

3. The clothes you wear to run matter more than you think

Surprise surprise, one glamorous effect of running you might not have known is chafing. When your skin rubs against itself or against certain fabrics and material, especially when you run in the heat, it can cause severe skin irritation and even scabbing afterward. Thankfully, I was blessed to have experienced chafing very minimally during my training, but when I did, it was primarily the result of the build of the clothes I wore. An ill-fitting sports bra leads to increased chafing as your underarm rubs against the material. Loose-fitting running shorts (think of pretty much any average female athletic short) can also cause chafing on your legs, especially when you run in the heat and your clothes become sweaty.

Chafing often hurts for days afterward and can even make it uncomfortable to run until your skin has healed, and so figuring out the cause of your chafing and finding a solution as soon as possible into your running journey will save you from a lot of pain. Because mine was caused by the loose-fitting nature of my running clothes, I then switched to skin-tight running shorts and snug sports bras. After I did this, my chafing completely went away and even come marathon day, I experienced none at all.

4. Your entire sleep schedule will change

This may be one that you’ve seen memes about, but I promise you, they are not an exaggeration. When I got into the thick of my marathon training, I literally had to stop saying yes to plans that started after 7pm because it would impact my ability to wake up early enough the next morning to go run.

One important note here is that due to my training being in the summer, I had to wake up earlier to run in order to “beat the heat.” This phenomenon doesn’t really apply during the fall and winter, but personally, I still prefer to wake up early to run so that I can complete my workout before I have to work all day.

Finding your routine during marathon training will likely result in you having to change your sleep schedule. Sleep is something you absolutely have to prioritize in your training, not just for proper rest, but also for recovery. My body runs on a schedule of waking up at 5am and going to sleep at 8:30pm and this is primarily due to my running habits.

5. Your caffeine consumption will likely go way up

Whether it be a little bit of caffeine to wake you up before your run or a big cup of coffee after your run to keep you awake the rest of the day, you will likely find that caffeine runs your life, unless you’re one of the crazy ones that doesn’t drink caffeine. I will admit that I have always been a big caffeine consumer, but running absolutely solidified this for me. It felt like there was always an excuse to drink more coffee. To be fair, caffeine does actually improve running performance, but one thing you may find after you begin training for your first marathon is that the caffeine consumption culture within the running community is strong (and frankly I wouldn’t change it!).

None of this made me regret signing up for the marathon. I just wish someone had warned me, so consider this your warning, and go for it anyway.

This story first appeared on vitalityritual.org.
